title: Lotus Sutra 5
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer finishes the Lotus Sutra by taking up chapter 20 and the story of the bodhisattva Never Disparaging, which the Buddha tells to the mahasattva Gainer of Great Authority. The story is set in the time of Awesome Sound King, the first of 20,000 million Buddhas who all bear that name, during an age when arrogant monks wield great authority. Never Disparaging does no study or recitation. He bows to everyone he meets and tells them they are certain to attain Buddhahood. Norman connects this to Ryokan, who bowed to pictures of farmers in the fields, and notes that people are disgusted by the monk and dismiss his predictions as vain and irresponsible.

sentences.text: Today we're going to finish the Lotus Sutra, starting with chapter 20.
In chapter 20 we have the story of the bodhisattva Never Disparaging.
That's this bodhisattva's name: Never Disparaging.
This is a really beautiful story, one of the high points for me in the Lotus Sutra.
The Buddha again is talking, as many of these chapters go.
He's telling a story about a Buddha who taught many, many, many kalpas ago.
He's telling this story to a mahasattva named Gainer of Great Authority.
*Gainer of Great Authority, long ago, in a measurable, boundless, inconceivable number of asamkhya kalpas in the past, there was a Buddha named Awesome Sound King.
Awesome Sound King.*
And this was a great Buddha, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
A lot of great things about him.
He lived his life, he passed away, and after that another Buddha appeared in the same land.
And what a coincidence: this Buddha's name was also Awesome Sound King.
Same name.
And the same thing happened.
He lived, he died.
Anyway, to make a long story short, this process continued until 20,000 million Buddhas had appeared, one after the other, all bearing the same name, Awesome Sound King.
Now, during that period of time, there were monks of overbearing arrogance, exercising great authority and power.
This was a bad period for the Dharma.
And it could be that whoever's speaking the words in the Lotus Sutra is thinking of their own time, in which maybe there also were monks of overbearing arrogance who exercised great authority.
Now, at the same time, there was a Bodhisattva monk named Never Disparaging.
Why was he named Never Disparaging?
Because whatever persons he happened to meet, monks, nuns, laymen or laywomen, he would bow in obeisance to them all, and he would speak words in obedience to them all.
He would bow in obeisance to them all, and he would speak words of praise.
And this is what he would say:
*I have profound reverence for you.
I would never dare treat you with this disparagement or arrogance.
Why?
Because you are all practicing the Bodhisattva way and are certain to attain Buddhahood.*

So whenever he met a person, he bowed to this person and he would say that, in this world in which most of the monks that he was encountering were very arrogant and exercised great authority and power.
Now this monk, Never Disparaging, did not study, did not recite scriptures.
All he did was go around bowing to people and saying this.
That was his entire practice.
He would say, "I would never dare disparage you because you are all certain to attain Buddhahood."
He repeated this, constantly bowing, hurling himself down, just bowing whenever he met anybody.
This must be where Ryokan got the idea of...

Ryokan used to go, in 18th century Japan, and wander among the fields, and when he would see a farmer, he would make a picture of the farmer, put it on a little altar, and bow in the fields to the farmer, to the picture of the farmer.
He must have gotten it from this Bodhisattva, Never Disparaging.
Now you would think that everybody would love this, but quite the opposite was the case.
People got very disgusted with him, and they really didn't like him at all.
They would say, "This ignorant monk, where does he come from?
Presuming to declare that he does not disparage us, and bestowing on us a prediction that we will attain Buddhahood.
We have no use for such vain and irresponsible predictions."
So they were not at all happy with him.
